findings.title: Remove unverified curl | sh of a remote install script
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 3 fetches https://example.com/install.sh with no version pin, checksum or signature, and pipes it straight into `sh`. It runs as root during the build. Whoever controls that URL, its DNS or its CDN can run any code in the image, and the code shipped can change from one build to the next with no change in the repo. The image layer keeps whatever that code does to the filesystem, and the image ships with /app. This is a supply-chain hole added by this PR.

findings.title: Fail the build when the install-script download fails
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL` has no `-f`, so a 404 or 500 error page goes to `sh` with curl exiting 0. If the connection breaks, curl's non-zero exit is still hidden: Alpine's /bin/sh (busybox ash) has no pipefail by default, so the RUN step's status comes from `sh`, not from curl. An empty or cut-off script can then 'succeed', or an HTML error page gets run as shell. Either way the build passes without the dependency the step is meant to install, and the image only breaks at runtime.

findings.title: Wait for result senders before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, Run sent every result before returning, so when it returned all len(jobs) values had been delivered, in job order. Now it starts one goroutine per job and returns right away, without a WaitGroup or any other way to wait for them. (1) The usual producer pattern `Run(ctx, jobs, ch); close(ch)` now closes the channel while goroutines are still sending, which panics with 'send on closed channel'. (2) A consumer that reads len(jobs) values and expects them in job order gets them in random order. (3) Run still ignores ctx. If the consumer stops reading or is cancelled, each pending sender blocks forever and that goroutine leaks. Before, only the caller's goroutine blocked. Run is exported, so this is a silent change to its behavior.

findings.title: Restore && so delete requires both admin and same tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: The base check required both `session.isAdmin` and `session.tenantId === record.tenantId`. With `||`, either one is now enough. (1) Cross-tenant bypass: an admin with session {isAdmin:true, tenantId:'A'} deleting record {tenantId:'B'} now gets true, where before it got false. (2) Privilege escalation: a non-admin with session {isAdmin:false, tenantId:'A'} deleting record {tenantId:'A'} now gets true, where before it got false. canDeleteRecord is the exported authorization check for deletes, so every caller gets the weaker check. The whole defect is visible in this one changed file.

findings.title: Stop parseSettings from hiding failures so updateFontSize can't save defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, invalid JSON or a bad field (e.g. raw='{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"16"}') made parseSettings throw. The error reached updateFontSize at src/settings.ts:20 and save() was never called. Now the catch at lines 14-15 returns { ...DEFAULTS } instead. updateFontSize sets fontSize and calls save(JSON.stringify({theme:'light',fontSize:size})), so the user's stored theme 'dark' is permanently replaced with the default. The catch also covers the JSON.parse SyntaxError, so a truncated or corrupt file is overwritten instead of reported. parseSettings is exported, so no caller can tell a real failure apart from a stored file that actually holds the default values.

findings.title: List artifacts at builtFrom's commit, not the "verified" ref
findings.whyItBreaks: `builtFrom` is still `build.ref(branch)`, but the artifacts now come from `build.artifactsAt(build.ref("verified"))`. When `branch` resolves to a different commit than `verified` (any branch other than verified), the report says it was built from commit A while listing artifacts from commit B. Callers of the exported buildReport get a report that contradicts itself, with artifacts from a commit they did not ask for. The `branch` argument no longer affects which artifacts are chosen.

findings.title: Restore the `limit` cap in recentEntries
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc comment at line 1 promises 'at most `limit` entries'. The new body only handles limit <= 0 and otherwise returns the whole reversed array, because the old `.slice(0, limit)` was removed. renderFeed (line 9) calls it with limit 20 and copies the result into `new Array(20)` using `i < page.length` (lines 10-11). With more than 20 entries, it writes past index 19 and the array grows, so the feed returns every entry instead of a 20-entry page.

findings.title: Use the filtered live count for the entry-count header
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR filters out stale entries (line 20) and writes rows only from `live` (line 21). Line 22 still passes `entries.length` to headerLines, and that value is written as `# entry-count: ${count}` (line 15). Example: 3 entries with 1 stale gives a header of `# entry-count: 3` above only 2 rows. The header and body of the exported manifest now disagree, so anything that reads the count to size or check the rows will see a wrong value or reject the file. Before this PR every entry was written, so the count was always right.

findings.title: Restore execute's return value instead of always throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: `execute(input: string): string` is exported and used to return `input.toUpperCase()`. The new body runs `throw new Error("always fails")` with no condition, so every call fails and the function can never return a string. Its `string` return type now promises something it never delivers. The repo has no in-repo callers, but this exported function is the module's only feature. Any outside caller that worked before will now get an exception on every call.

findings.title: Don't reject viewers in isEligible; it breaks handle()'s read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: handle() calls isEligible at line 24 before it checks the viewer role at line 25. Before this change, an active viewer with attempts < 5 passed isEligible and got "read-only". Now line 18 returns false for any viewer, so handle() returns "rejected" and the `req.role === "viewer"` branch at line 25 can never run. The new guard blocks the viewer read-only access that handle() still clearly intends to allow. The exported isEligible contract also changes: viewers are no longer eligible.

findings.title: Don't require payment to save a draft
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed() is the only check for two different actions: submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). The new `&& order.payment === "paid"` clause applies to both. For {state:"draft", payment:"missing"}, canProceed used to return true and now returns false, so saveDraft now returns "blocked" instead of "saved". Payment status has nothing to do with saving a draft, and an unpaid order is exactly the normal case for one. Users can no longer save their in-progress, unpaid orders.

findings.title: Use the channel head's files, not stable's, in publishSnapshot
findings.whyItBreaks: The snapshot sets `commit: head` (the head of the requested `channel`, line 13/16), but `files` now comes from `repo.filesAt(stable)` (lines 14/18). For any channel other than `stable`, such as DEFAULT_CHANNEL `main`, the published Snapshot claims commit X but lists the files at the stable head. Before this change, `files` came from `filesAt(head)`, so this is a regression in an exported function, and the bug is visible within this one file.

findings.title: Honor the new `limit` parameter instead of hardcoded max_count
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff adds `limit=10` to the public `build()` signature, which tells callers they can choose how many items come back. The body never reads `limit`. The loop still runs over `range(max_count)`, and `max_count` is hardcoded to 10 (lines 2 and 4). So `build('x', limit=3)` returns 10 items and `build('x', limit=50)` returns 10 items. A caller that sizes or caps its work by `limit` gets the wrong output and no error. `build` is a public, non-underscore function, so this broken contract is already shipping even though nothing in the repo calls it yet.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int or drop the promise
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public name says the function returns a positive int, but the body is just `int(value)`. So parse_positive_int("-5") returns -5 and parse_positive_int("0") returns 0, with no error. charge() (line 6) is now written as if its input were already checked, and it multiplies straight into cents: charge("-5") returns -500. total_cents() then adds that up, so negative charges can silently cancel out real ones (total_cents(["10","-10"]) == 0). The name tells callers they can skip their own checks, but nothing is actually checked.

findings.title: Restore defensive copy; apply_values now mutates caller's DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version ran `result = df.copy()` and wrote only to `result`, so the caller's `df` was never changed. The new version runs `df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value` directly on the argument and returns that same object. Any caller that keeps using the original frame after `out = apply_values(df, m)` now finds its `value` column overwritten. If the input has no `value` column, one is added to the caller's frame and filled with NaN for unmatched rows. Because `out is df`, a caller can no longer compare before and after. The function is public, so this silently breaks callers who relied on it not changing their input. This is data corruption, not a style issue.

findings.title: Make parse_positive_int reject non-positive and unparseable input
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public name says the result is a positive integer, but the body is still `s.parse().unwrap_or(0)`. It parses any i64, so "-5" becomes -5. Any parse failure ("abc", "", "1.5", an overflowing value) becomes 0, which is not positive either. `charge` (line 6) relies on the name and does no checks of its own, so `charge("-5")` returns -500 (a negative charge, i.e. a refund) and `charge("abc")` returns 0 instead of reporting an error. The rename makes the missing check look like it exists, so new callers will skip their own validation.

findings.title: Borrow in dbg! so items is not moved before items.len()
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!` takes its argument by value and returns it. `dbg!(items);` moves the `Vec<String>` into the macro, then drops the returned value at the semicolon. `items.len()` on line 3 then uses a moved value (rustc E0382, borrow of moved value), so `process` and the whole crate stop compiling. Separately, `dbg!` is debug output that writes to stderr, and it was left in a public function.

findings.title: Compute changedPaths from the same revision reported as fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset doc comment (src/changeset.ts:7-8) says fromRevision is the revision the changed paths were computed against, and that consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly that revision. After this change, fromRevision is still store.resolve(pinnedTag), but changedPaths comes from store.readChangedPaths(store.resolve("latest")). Whenever the pinned tag and 'latest' resolve to different revisions, consumers replay a path set taken from a different base onto the pinned revision. Paths changed between the pinned revision and latest get left out, and the result is wrong. The function is exported and nothing in the returned object signals the mismatch.

findings.title: Update readers of users.email before renaming the column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, users no longer has an `email` column. src/query.sql:1 (`SELECT email FROM users;`) is unchanged and will fail with an unknown-column error. The rename also happens in one step, so code deployed before the migration still reads `email` while code deployed after needs `contact_email`. Nothing in the repo keeps the old name working, so there is no safe deploy order.

findings.title: Remove hardcoded live billing API key from source
findings.whyItBreaks: The `bk_live_` secret is written into the source file. Anyone who can read the repo, its git history, forks, CI logs or built bundles can see it and act on the production billing API with this account's credentials. Every environment (dev, test, staging) would also call the live endpoint with the production key. Merging the change exposes the key permanently in history, so the key has to be rotated even if this commit is reverted.

findings.title: Fix inverted admin check that lets non-admins purge projects
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code only deleted when `user.isAdmin && project.archived`. The new line 12 returns "forbidden" when `user.isAdmin` is true, so the authorization check is flipped. With {isAdmin:false} and {archived:true}, line 12 passes, line 13 passes, and line 14 runs db.delete: a non-admin can permanently destroy project data. With {isAdmin:true} and {archived:true}, the call returns "forbidden", so the admin purge feature stops working.

findings.title: Restore default settings when config file is missing
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() returns None when the path does not exist (app/config.py:6-7). The diff removes the `if settings is None` fallback, so startup() now runs `None["workers"]` at line 14 and raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable`. Before this change, a missing config file started the app with workers=1 and region=us-east-1. Now startup fails with an error that nothing catches.

findings.title: Propagate gateway Submit error instead of logging and returning nil
findings.whyItBreaks: `Charge` is exported and returns `error`. When `gw.Submit` fails (declined card, network or gateway error), the new code only calls `log.Printf` (line 17) and then reaches `return nil` (line 19). Every caller gets the same result for a failed charge and a successful one, so it will treat an unpaid charge as paid (fulfil orders, mark invoices settled). Before this change the error reached the caller wrapped as `charge failed: %w`. The function still returns an error for invalid amounts but not for real payment failures, so its contract is inconsistent.

findings.title: Include tenantId in settings cache key to stop cross-tenant leaks
findings.whyItBreaks: cacheKey(name) returns `settings:${name}` and ignores tenantId. settingsFor(tenantA, 'x') fetches A's value and caches it under 'settings:x' (line 16). A later settingsFor(tenantB, 'x') finds that entry at lines 13-14 and returns tenant A's value without calling store.fetch(tenantB, ...). One tenant's settings leak to another, and tenant B never gets its own value.

findings.title: Restore tenantId parameter on exported invalidate()
findings.whyItBreaks: invalidate is exported and changed from (tenantId, name) to (name). Existing callers outside this repo that call invalidate(tenantId, name) now pass tenantId as the name, so the wrong key is deleted and stale values stay cached (TypeScript callers fail to compile). With the new shared key, invalidating also clears the entry for every tenant at once, so per-tenant invalidation is no longer possible.

findings.title: Fix reserve race that oversells stock across the awaited save
findings.whyItBreaks: `remaining` is read at line 15, before the `await this.store.save(...)` at line 17. The in-memory decrement only happens at line 18, after the await finishes. Example with stock=1: two overlapping `reserve('A')` calls both read remaining=1, both pass the `<= 0` check, both call save('A', 0) and both return true. Two reservations succeed for one unit. With stock=N, any number of overlapping calls can succeed, and every one saves the same N-1, so the stored count is also wrong. Before this PR, reserve was synchronous and the check and decrement could not be interleaved.

findings.title: Update retry() for backoff() now returning milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() used to return seconds (Math.min(30, 2**attempt)). It now returns milliseconds (Math.min(30_000, 2**attempt*1000)). poll.ts was updated to match, but the other caller, src/jobs/retry.ts:12, still runs `sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`. For a=0 it now sleeps 1,000,000 ms (about 16.7 min) instead of 1 s. For a>=5 it sleeps 30,000,000 ms (about 8.3 h) instead of 30 s. Any retry() call effectively hangs, and so does whatever job or request is awaiting it.

findings.title: Propagate f.Close() error instead of discarding it in defer
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, Save returned f.Close()'s error on success (`return f.Close()`). Now `defer f.Close()` (line 13) throws that error away and Save returns w.Flush()'s result (line 20). On NFS, FUSE, quota or full-disk filesystems, a delayed write failure often only shows up at close. In that case Save returns nil for a truncated or unwritten file, and callers can't tell it apart from a real save. Save is exported, so every external caller gets success for a failed save.

findings.title: Fix off-by-one in page_window that drops each page's last row
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) range, with end = min(start + page_size, row_count) (lines 17-21). Iterating range(start, end - 1) at line 28 therefore leaves out index end-1. Before this change the loop was range(start, end). Example: rows=['a','b','c'], page_size=2. Page 0 now returns ['a'] instead of ['a','b'], and page 1 returns [] instead of ['c']. A page_size of 1 always gives empty pages. render_page calls page_window at lib/pagination.py:40, and summarize calls render_page at lib/pagination.py:52, so every rendered page and the summary silently lose rows.

findings.title: Restore TTL comparison so fresh entries are returned, not stale ones
findings.whyItBreaks: With `>`, an entry still within its TTL (age <= ttlMs) falls through to `this.entries.delete(key); return null` at lines 21-22. Every fresh read is a miss and also deletes the entry. Entries older than ttlMs are returned at line 19 and never evicted. The cache now does the opposite of its TTL contract: it serves expired data and never returns valid data.

findings.title: Stop splicing while iterating; consecutive done jobs are skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.forEach moves to index+1 after each callback. When `jobs.splice(index, 1)` removes a done job, the next element shifts into `index` and is never checked. Two adjacent done jobs therefore leave the second one in the array: [d1,d2,p] -> [d2,p]. The function also now mutates and returns the caller's array instead of returning a new filtered array. That is a public contract change: any caller still holding the original array sees it modified.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in rankScores sort
findings.whyItBreaks: With no comparator, sort() turns each number into a string and sorts by UTF-16 code units. Example: scores [9, 10, 100] sort to [10, 100, 9], then reverse to [9, 100, 10]. With n=1 the cutoff is 9, so the filter keeps every player with score >= 9 in input order, and slice(0,1) can return the score-9 player instead of the score-100 one. With n=2 the cutoff is 100, which drops the second-best player (10). Negative and fractional scores also sort wrongly as strings. The base code used (a, b) => b - a, so this is a regression in the exported topPlayers (src/leaderboard.ts:15 cutoff) and in formatBoard (src/leaderboard.ts:20).

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison for webhook HMAC verification
findings.whyItBreaks: `verify` now checks the attacker-supplied signature against the expected HMAC hex digest with `==`. Python's `==` on strings stops at the first byte that differs, so the response time shows how many leading characters of the guess are right. An attacker can measure many requests and recover the valid signature for a chosen payload one hex character at a time, without knowing the secret. `handle` (app/webhook.py:14) is the only authentication gate before `processor(payload)` runs, so a forged signature means arbitrary payloads get processed. The base version used `hmac.compare_digest`, which takes the same time regardless of where the strings differ, so this is a security regression introduced by this PR.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base version, the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs ran inside one `with db.transaction():` block, so all three committed or rolled back together. At HEAD, only `_record_ledger` (line 23) is inside the block, which commits when it exits. `_apply_balances` (line 24) then runs outside the transaction. If either UPDATE fails (constraint error, lost connection, crash, or the process is killed between the two statements), the ledger row is already committed with no balance change. The debit (lines 9-12) can also be applied with no credit (lines 13-16), so money is lost. Together the three writes can no longer be undone as a unit.

findings.title: Restore UTC getters in billingDay to keep billing days timezone-stable
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code used getUTCFullYear, getUTCMonth and getUTCDate. The new line uses getFullYear, getMonth and getDate, which read the process's local timezone. On any host not set to UTC, an instant near midnight UTC gets a different day. Example: new Date('2026-11-21T23:30:00Z') returns '2026-11-21' in UTC but '2026-11-22' with TZ=Asia/Tokyo. The same timestamp can land on a different billing day on different servers. sameBillingDay (line 8) now gives wrong answers too: two instants on the same UTC day can compare unequal, and instants on different UTC days can compare equal. Day keys written under the old UTC rule won't match the new ones for records near midnight. The diff looks like a refactor, but it changes behavior.

findings.title: Include tenant in profile memo key to prevent cross-tenant leaks
findings.whyItBreaks: `memo` is a module-level Map (line 7) shared across all calls. With `key = account`, calling `readProfile('A', 'u1', f)` caches A's profile under 'u1'. A later `readProfile('B', 'u1', f)` hits `memo.get('u1')` at line 15 and returns tenant A's Profile (including `tenant: 'A'` and A's displayName) without ever calling `fetchProfile('B','u1')`. That leaks data across tenants and returns the wrong profile.

findings.title: Don't swallow missing-key error in load(); "" is a valid stored value
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, load() threw `missing: ${key}` when store.get(key) returned undefined. Now the try/catch at lines 2-8 catches that throw and returns "". The store is Map<string,string>, so "" is a value a key can really hold. A caller can't tell a missing key from a key set to "". loadAll (src/store.ts:12) used to stop on the first missing key; now it returns a full-length array with "" in place of each missing key. Both functions are exported, so this changes the public error contract for outside callers too. The catch has no binding and no logging, so nothing records the failure.

findings.title: Keep Config.timeoutMs; renaming it and adding required field breaks callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported. Before this PR it was {maxAttempts, timeoutMs}. Now it is {maxAttempts, retries, timeout}. Every TS caller that builds a Config stops compiling: timeoutMs is now an unknown property and retries/timeout are missing. JS callers, or callers whose config is loaded from JSON or persisted settings, still pass timeoutMs, so config.timeout is undefined. Then Date.now() + undefined is NaN, `Date.now() > NaN` is always false (line 10), and the deadline silently stops working. Nothing errors.

findings.title: Stop retryBackground from treating zero retries as zero calls
findings.whyItBreaks: The new field is named `retries`, which means extra attempts after the first. The loop `for (i = 0; i < config.retries; i++)` treats it as the total number of attempts instead. With retries=0 ('no retries'), fn is never called, and the function still returns normally as if it succeeded. With retries=N, fn runs N times, not N+1.

findings.title: Surface the final failure from public retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground is a newly exported function. Its `catch { continue; }` throws away every error. When attempts run out, or the deadline at line 23 is hit, it returns void, exactly as it does on success. External callers have no way to tell whether fn ever succeeded.

findings.title: Handle number values instead of reading .length on string | number
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 2 widens `value` to `string | number`. Line 6 then reads `value.length`, but numbers have no `length`. Under TypeScript this fails with TS2339 ("Property 'length' does not exist on type 'string | number'"). In plain JS or loosely checked code, a number value renders the text `len=undefined`.

findings.title: Restore rendering the field value instead of a len= label
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the input's defaultValue was `value`. Now it is `len=<n>`, so the user's existing value is replaced by a debug-style length string. Any form that reads this input would submit `len=5` where it used to submit the real value.

findings.title: Stop printing secrets.TOKEN to the build log
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 12 runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, which writes the secret straight to stdout. GitHub hides a secret in logs only when the exact registered value appears. Changed copies, such as parts of a multi-line secret or transformed values, are not hidden, so masking is the only protection here. The workflow runs `on: push` (line 2), so this step runs on every push. TOKEN is set only in this step's `env:`, so `make build` (line 13) never gets it. The step does nothing except write the secret to the log.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git spawnSync so large PR diffs don't fail review
findings.whyItBreaks: Without maxBuffer, spawnSync uses Node's default of 1 MiB (1024*1024). The full PR patch is captured through this helper (`git diff mergeBase headSha` @140), and so is `git diff --name-only` @57. When stdout goes over 1 MiB, Node kills the child with ENOBUFS and res.status comes back null. The `res.status !== 0` check @38 then throws, runGithub's catch @182-193 posts a 'review failed' check, and the process sets exitCode=1. Any PR with a patch over 1 MiB, which worked before under the 64 MiB limit, now always fails CI. The gh helpers @19 and @29 still use 64 MiB, so only git is affected.

findings.title: Send mergeBase as bundle.baseSha to match patch and changedFiles
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch @140 and changedFiles @141 are computed from `mergeBase` (@139), but the bundle now sends `baseSha`. That value is the PR base branch tip (PR_BASE_SHA, or the origin/main merge-base fallback @138). Once main has moved past the branch point, these are different commits. The bundle then labels the patch base..head, but the diff's real base is mergeBase. Anything that re-derives the diff from the bundle SHAs will see main's later commits reverted as if the PR changed them.

findings.title: Restore explicit read-only sandbox for codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex starts `codex exec` with cwd=opts.repoPath (line 24) and a prompt built from the untrusted repo and diff. Before this change, `-s read-only` pinned the sandbox, so the agent could not write files or run mutating commands no matter what config was in place. With the flag gone, the sandbox comes from Codex's config resolution instead. If a user has `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"` or `"danger-full-access"` in ~/.codex/config.toml, or a profile or env setting does the same, that mode now applies here. Instructions planted in the reviewed repo could then edit files in the checkout or run code from it. That is exactly the injection and sandbox-violation risk a reviewer must rule out. The function is exported, so every caller gets this weaker guarantee.

findings.title: Restore merge-base normalization before diffing against PR_BASE_SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: baseSha comes from process.env.PR_BASE_SHA when it is set (line 138). In GitHub Actions that is normally pull_request.base.sha, the current tip of the base branch, not where the PR branched off. The old code ran `git merge-base baseSha headSha` and diffed from that point. The new code diffs and lists files straight from `baseSha..HEAD` with a two-dot diff. When main has moved since the branch point, every change merged to main in between shows up in `patch` as an inverse change, and in `changedFiles`/`changedPaths` as a touched file. The reviewer then gets files and hunks the PR never touched, may report findings on them, and inlineComments (line 63) will post comments on those paths because changedPaths now contains them. Only the fallback branch (no env var) still uses a merge base, so the env-var path regresses.

findings.title: Diff the PR head SHA, not HEAD, so the patch matches the reviewed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: headSha can come from PR_HEAD_SHA (line 137). It is passed as bundle.headSha (line 165) and used as commit_id for the review and as head_sha for the check run (lines 85 and 124). The patch now diffs against `HEAD` instead. When the checked-out HEAD differs from PR_HEAD_SHA, the reviewed patch belongs to a different commit than the one the review and check are attached to. This happens with the default pull_request checkout of refs/pull/N/merge, or with any detached checkout. Inline comment line numbers can then fail to resolve on the commit_id commit. The POST is rejected, the catch fallback (lines 96-108) re-posts without comments, and all inline comments are silently dropped. The old code diffed headSha explicitly.

findings.title: Restore function replacers so `$` patterns in the diff aren't expanded
findings.whyItBreaks: When the second argument to String.prototype.replace is a string, JS reads `$$`, `$&`, `` $` `` and `$'` inside it as special patterns. With a function replacer they are left alone. The inserted values are attacker/author-controlled: `JSON.stringify(bundle)` holds the whole patch, `bundle.patch` is the raw diff, and `candidate` is model output. Code under review often contains these sequences, e.g. bash `$$` (PID) and `$'\n'`, or JS regex replacements like `'$&'`. What each one does: `$$` collapses to `$`. `$&` turns into the literal placeholder token. `` $` `` and `$'` splice in the whole prompt text before or after the placeholder. So the reviewer and critic models see a diff that differs from what was actually changed. They can then miss real defects, or flag code that isn't there. The function replacers this PR removes existed exactly to prevent that.

findings.title: Restore commit_id pin in fallback review POST
findings.whyItBreaks: postReview reviews the diff mergeBase..headSha (runGithub @src/adapters/github.ts:141-144). The main path pins `commit_id: headSha` (line 89), and the base version of the fallback did too. The fallback now sends only event and body. GitHub's create-review API treats a missing commit_id as 'use the PR's latest commit'. So if new commits land between checkout and posting, the fallback attaches a REQUEST_CHANGES/COMMENT verdict to code Needlefish never reviewed. Both paths also now disagree on which commit they pin: postCheck still uses head_sha=headSha (line 128) while the fallback review floats to the newest commit. The fallback runs whenever the JSON post fails, most often because an inline comment line is invalid, so this is a live path.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of defaulting them to P1
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code threw an error for any of these: a bad severity or category, an empty file, title, whyItBreaks or suggestedFix, or a line number that was not a positive number. The new code (lines 95-110) turns each of those into a normal-looking value. An invalid or missing severity becomes "P1", which is a blocking severity. An unknown category becomes "bug". A missing file becomes "". lineStart becomes 0, or NaN for input like "abc". The fix fields become empty strings. Callers get back a valid `Finding` and cannot tell it apart from a real one. So a garbage or truncated model reply now produces a fake P1 finding with no file or line, when it used to fail validation. Category is also no longer trimmed: " security " used to normalize to "security" and is now silently rewritten to "bug". A null or non-object element now throws a TypeError when `raw.severity` is read (line 96), instead of the old descriptive error.

findings.title: Restore lenient mode so malformed findings are dropped, not invented
findings.whyItBreaks: `normalizeReview(raw, strict = true)` is exported. With strict=false it promised to drop malformed findings and keep the valid ones. The parameter has been removed (line 113, line 131). JavaScript ignores extra arguments, so existing `normalizeReview(x, false)` calls still run, but their behavior changes with no warning. Malformed findings are no longer dropped: they come back as fake P1/'bug' findings (lines 98-105). A null entry in `findings` now throws a TypeError at line 96 and fails the whole review, where it used to be skipped.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo for gh pr view in the pre-checkout step
findings.whyItBreaks: The 'Resolve PR refs' step (lines 26-40) runs before 'Checkout PR head' (line 42). Without `-R`, and with no `GH_REPO` set in the step env (lines 28-32) or anywhere else in the workflow, `gh pr view` works out which repo to use from the git remote in the current directory. On a clean workspace there is no git repo yet, so gh fails with 'not a git repository'. On a reused self-hosted workspace it reads whatever stale checkout is there. The call sits inside `$(...)` as an argument to `echo`, so a failed gh call does not stop the step under `bash -e`, and `head=`/`base=` get written as empty strings. With an empty `ref`, actions/checkout falls back to the workflow_dispatch ref (usually main). `PR_HEAD_SHA`/`PR_BASE_SHA` then reach the review step empty (lines 56-57). Result: manual reviews quietly check the wrong commit or fail later with an unclear error. This only affects workflow_dispatch; pull_request events take the EVENT_HEAD branch.

findings.title: Restore malformed-output errors in normalizeReview instead of empty defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, normalizeReview threw 'malformed review output: ...' when the input was not an object, when summary was not a string, or when findings, checked or residual_risks was not an array. Now every one of those failures turns into a value. Bad input such as null, a truncated or garbage model response, or {findings: 'oops'} becomes {summary:'', findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}. That is the same shape as a real review with nothing to report. A caller cannot tell 'the reviewer produced unusable output' apart from 'the reviewer found no defects and no blocking risks', so a broken review run gets read as PASS. The function is exported and is the public contract for checking review output, so every caller is forced to accept this, even though no file in the repo calls it yet. Malformed findings or residual_risks are the worst case: real reported issues get dropped without any signal.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for workflow_dispatch runs
findings.whyItBreaks: On a workflow_dispatch run, `github.event.pull_request` is empty. Line 29 therefore resolves to `github.ref`, so the job checks out the branch the dispatch ran on instead of the PR head. Line 35 falls back to the hard-coded 'main', so any PR that targets another base branch is diffed against the wrong base. Lines 45-46 set PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA to empty strings. Before this change, the removed 'Resolve PR refs' step looked up headRefOid, baseRefOid and baseRef with `gh pr view $PR_NUM` for exactly this case. Now the manual trigger the workflow advertises on line 13 ("PR number to review") reviews the wrong code or gets no SHAs. Pull_request-event runs are unaffected.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git() so diffs over 1 MiB don't abort review
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync uses a 1 MiB maxBuffer by default. Before this change git() raised it to 64 MiB (gh() at lines 33-37 still does). runLocal gets the whole patch through git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]) at line 100. With the default limit, any diff over 1 MiB (a lockfile change, vendored code, generated files) makes Node kill git with ENOBUFS. That leaves res.status null, so `res.status !== 0` throws. The error text only uses res.stderr, which is empty here, so the user sees `git diff <sha> HEAD failed: ` with no reason. Large PRs that reviewed fine before now cannot be reviewed. The same applies to the --name-only call at line 101 on very large changesets.

score.error: malformed finding: blocking finding has low confidence

findings.title: Restore trusted-tool checkout; don't run PR head code as the reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, the tool ran from frankekn/needlefish@main in a separate `needlefish/` directory and the PR head was only read from `target/`. Now the PR head is checked out at the workspace root. `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` uses the PR's own package.json and lockfile, and lifecycle scripts are allowed. Then `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` runs the PR's own src/ with GH_TOKEN, which has pull-requests: write and checks: write (lines 16-19). This happens on `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 23). As a result, any PR can (a) change src/ so it posts a PASS review or check for itself, which defeats the review gate the old header comment was written to protect, and (b) run arbitrary code on the persistent self-hosted host and steal the write token. The same-repo guard on line 24 is skipped for workflow_dispatch. In that path the head SHA comes from `gh pr view` for any PR number, so manually dispatching on a fork PR also runs that fork's code.

findings.title: Restore severity trim/uppercase and keep fail-safe P1 fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, line 96 ran `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()`. That turned inputs like "p0", "p1" and " P2 " into valid severities. Unknown or missing values became P1, which errs toward blocking. Now `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity)` compares the raw value exactly. Any case or whitespace difference fails the check and the finding becomes P3. So a reviewer that outputs "p0" (data loss) now produces a P3 finding, the lowest severity. A missing or garbled severity also becomes P3, so callers can't tell a failed parse from a real low-severity finding. normalizeFinding is exported and normalizeReview applies it to every finding (line 132), so every consumer gets the downgraded severity.

findings.title: Restore scrubbing of GitHub tokens from the codex child env
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes the env copy that removed GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN, and drops the `env` option from spawnSync. When spawnSync gets no `env`, Node passes the parent's full process.env to the child, so the codex process now inherits those GitHub credentials. That process runs with cwd set to the repo under review and gets a prompt containing untrusted diff and repo content. A prompt injection in a reviewed PR can make the agent run read-only commands such as `env`, `printenv` or `gh auth token` and print the token. The output then comes back through runCodex as review text, which may be posted or logged. The `-s read-only` sandbox limits writes; it does not stop the agent from reading environment variables. Before this change the tokens never reached the child process.

findings.title: Restore same-repo guard before running PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The job runs on `pull_request` (line 8) on a `self-hosted` runner (line 18). It checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (line 23), then runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28) and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34), both under `zsh -l` login shells. All of that code comes from the PR. The removed `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only thing stopping fork PRs from triggering this job. Without it, anyone who opens a fork PR can edit package.json lifecycle scripts, the lockfile or src/ and run arbitrary commands as the runner user. Self-hosted runners are not ephemeral, so an attacker can leave persistent backdoors, read host credentials that the login shell loads, and tamper with later trusted jobs. The read-only fork token and withheld secrets do not limit any of this.

findings.title: Explicit 0 ms runner grace/give-up value is now silently replaced by the default
findings.whyItBreaks: readRunnerDurationMs parses NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS (lines 3-6, fallback 5000) and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS (lines 7-10, fallback 2000). Before this change, `parsed >= 0` accepted "0". At line 124 that meant SIGKILL right after SIGTERM, and at line 123 it meant giving up right after SIGKILL. With `parsed > 0`, "0" now gets the same fallback as an invalid value. So a setup that explicitly asked for no grace now waits 5s+2s on every timeout, and nothing tells the user their setting was ignored.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so unmapped changed files are still reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code added a 'tail-coverage' hotspot for every changed file that no selected hotspot covered. That code is gone, so only files inside the first MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 hotspots get a deep review (line 26, sliced at line 93). Two kinds of file now get no deep review at all: a changed file the map model forgot to assign, and a file that was only in a hotspot ranked 7th or lower. Nothing records the skip in checked or residual_risks, so deriveVerdict (line 122) can return PASS on code nobody looked at.

findings.title: Propagate deep-pass residual_risks instead of hardcoding []
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass returns `res.residual_risks`, which can include blocks:true risks. The old code collected these into `residuals` and passed them to the critic. The new code only reads `res.findings` and `res.summary`, and sets `residual_risks: []` in candidateMerged (line 113). Blocking risks from the deep passes therefore never reach the critic, `pruned.residual_risks` usually leaves them out, and deriveVerdict (line 122) can return PASS. A deep pass that says 'I cannot conclude' now looks the same as a clean one.

findings.title: Keep a body component in the dedup key to avoid merging distinct findings
findings.whyItBreaks: The dedup key used to include the first 80 normalized characters of whyItBreaks. It is now only file|lineStart|category plus the first 60 characters of the title (line 37). Two separate findings on the same line, with the same category and a generic title, now get the same key. Only one survives (the higher severity, or the first seen), and the other is dropped before the critic sees it.

findings.title: Restore focus substitution in deep-pass prompt for large PRs
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, the deep prompt filled `{{FOCUS}}` with `bundle.focus ?? "(none)"`. That line is now gone. The template probably still contains the placeholder, since the base code filled it in. If so, every per-hotspot deep review now receives the literal text `{{FOCUS}}` and never sees the user's focus. reviewSmall still sends the whole bundle, focus included (line 52-55), so the same `focus` input works for small PRs and is silently dropped for large ones (more than 10 files or patch over 30000 chars, line 30-31).

findings.title: Keep focus/deep in the map-pass bundle for large PRs
findings.whyItBreaks: `focus` and `deep` were removed from mapBundle, so the map pass (which picks hotspots, sorts them, and keeps only the top MAX_HOTSPOTS=6) can no longer weight hotspots by the user's focus or the deep flag. A focused or deep request on a large PR is now handled exactly like a default one, and the focused area can fall outside the 6 selected hotspots. Small PRs still see both fields through the full bundle.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes to avoid '1m 60s' output
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are now floored from raw ms, and the remainder is rounded to seconds separately. Any remainder of 59500ms or more rounds to 60 with no carry. Examples: ms=119600 gives minutes=1, seconds=round(59.6)=60, so the output is '1m 60s' (old code gave '2m 0s'). ms=59600 gives minutes=0, seconds=60, so the output is '60s' (old code gave '1m 0s'). This text appears in the per-call stats and the total duration in renderMarkdown (src/shared/render.ts:75 and :80).

findings.title: Restore rejection of 0 in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The function is exported. Its name and its error message (`${label} requires a positive integer`, line 33) promise a value > 0. Changing `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` at line 32 means `Number("0")` now passes. `Number("")` and `Number("  ")` also evaluate to 0, so empty or whitespace-only input (for example an unset env var or a flag with no value) is now returned as 0 instead of throwing. Callers receive a different result (0 returned instead of an error) even though the promise is unchanged. You can see this within the single changed file.
